scenes.headline: ₹90 per dollar.
scenes.subtext: All-time low in 2025. Crisis — or correction?

scenes.title: What does 'rupee falling' actually mean?
scenes.body: The rupee's value against the dollar is just a price — determined by supply and demand, like any market. When more people want dollars than rupees, the dollar becomes expensive. That's depreciation.
scenes.analogy: Think of it like apples. If everyone wants apples and there aren't many, the price goes up. Currency works exactly the same way.

zones.label: Strong rupee — imports cheaper, exports costly
Stable zone — manageable for both sides
Weakening — oil bill rises, IT sector profits

scenes.title: Why does it fall?
scenes.intro: Five forces pulled the rupee to ₹90 in 2025. Tap each to understand it.

items.title: Trade deficit — we import more than we export
items.detail: India's exports fell 11.8% in Oct 2025 while imports surged 16.6%. Every import is paid in dollars. More dollar demand = weaker rupee.
items.stat: $206B spent on oil + gold alone in FY26

items.title: FPI outflows — foreign money leaving
items.detail: Foreign Portfolio Investors sell Indian stocks, convert rupees to dollars, and leave. This floods the market with rupees.

items.title: Strong dollar — global, not India-specific
items.detail: When US Fed raises rates, global money flows toward dollar investments. Every currency weakens — not just the rupee.

items.title: Gold imports — India's expensive habit
items.detail: India is the world's 2nd largest gold consumer. Gold imports grew ~200% in Oct 2025, widening the current account deficit.

items.title: Sentiment — fear becomes self-fulfilling
items.detail: If traders expect the rupee to fall, they rush to buy dollars now. That expectation itself causes the fall.

scenes.title: Not everyone loses

left_items.label: IT & software exporters
left_items.detail: Earn in dollars, spend in rupees — more profit

left_items.label: NRIs sending remittances
left_items.detail: Their dollars buy more rupees for family

left_items.label: Textile & garment exporters
left_items.detail: Indian goods cheaper for foreign buyers

right_items.label: Oil importers & consumers
right_items.detail: Same oil, more rupees — petrol prices rise

right_items.label: Common man via inflation
right_items.detail: Costlier imports = higher prices for all

scenes.officer_framing: Rupee depreciation redistributes advantage — the real question is whether India's export gains outweigh its import inflation. With $250B+ in IT exports and $120B in NRI remittances, India has structural buffers.

scenes.title: The big picture — India is not collapsing
scenes.body: The rupee has depreciated from ₹17 to ₹90 since 1991 — that's 34 years at ~4.5% per year. This is structural, not sudden. India remains one of the fastest-growing major economies with strong forex reserves.

timeline.event: Fixed exchange rate — govt pegged rupee to dollar
India nearly ran out of dollars. Had to pledge gold with IMF.
Switched to managed float — market determines rate, RBI prevents chaos
Rupee hits ₹90. RBI shifts from defending levels to managing volatility.

scenes.title: Use this in SSB
scenes.pi_question: What do you think about the falling rupee?
scenes.gd_line: Rupee depreciation is a double-edged sword — while it raises import inflation, it makes Indian exports more competitive and boosts IT sector earnings. The concern is not the direction, but the pace of the fall.
lecturette_structure: Open: ₹90 per dollar — historical low in 2025. Crisis or correction?
What it means: supply-demand of currencies, depreciation vs devaluation
Why it happened: trade deficit, FPI outflows, strong dollar
Two sides: IT gains vs import inflation — balanced view
Close: India's forex reserves and structural resilience — managed descent, not free fall
scenes.pi_answer: Sir, a falling rupee reflects structural realities — our trade deficit, global dollar strength, and capital flow dynamics. It's not inherently bad — our IT sector earns $250B+ annually in dollars, and NRI remittances hit $120B+. The real question is whether RBI can manage the pace of depreciation, and with $650B in forex reserves, India has the firepower to do that.
scenes.one_liner: The rupee's fall is a managed descent — the goal isn't to hold the parachute shut, it's to make sure it opens at the right time.

questions.q: Someone in GD says: 'The falling rupee is a sign of India's economic failure.' Your response?
options: Agree — a weak currency always signals weakness
That's one dimension — but rupee depreciation also boosts IT exports, NRI remittances, and tourism. The key is managing the pace, not stopping the fall.
Disagree — a falling rupee is completely fine
questions.explanation: Balance is the OLQ response. Never take an extreme position on a complex economic topic in GD.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism that weakens the rupee?
options: Dollar demand exceeds supply in forex markets — due to trade deficits, FPI outflows, or a globally strong dollar
questions.explanation: Currency value is fundamentally a supply-demand story in the forex market. This is the clean one-liner for PI.
